newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Volatile platinum hinges on Russia sales - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Volatile platinum hinges on Russia sales - analysts.

text.p: Expected lower Russian platinum sales due to dwindling stockpiles could continue to support the metal's upward climb, analysts said on Friday.
The platinum price -- usually trading at a premium to gold -- has been tracking gold closely for several weeks but began moving away from the yellow metal mid-week.
On Friday platinum was more than $20 higher than gold. By 1100 GMT, it was trading at $366 an ounce to gold's $342.50.
"If platinum starts recognising its own fundamentals then it should move away from gold," said a Johannesburg platinum analyst.
Analysts said the white metal was also higher on the increased palladium price and uncertainty about Russian supplies.
The South African platinum industry -- the world's largest -- recently predicted that Russian stockpiles would run out soon.
Analysts and industry officials said Russian sales this year had slowed considerably which, coupled with strong fundamentals, helped platinum's upward climb.

"I think much will depend on what the Russians do but at this stage of the game it looks like they have slowed down sales. I think in the short term we can see firm prices," the Johannesburg analyst said.
Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd, producer of about 36 percent of the world's newly-mined platinum, said last month it expected Russian stockpiles to run out in the near future.

"It would seem as if there is now some possibility that we're getting to the end of that (Russian stockpiles). It seems as if this year the Russians will be selling less", a senior industry official said.
Russian platinum production is estimated to be between 600,000 to 700,000 ounces but the size of its stockpiles are a closely-guarded secret.

Precious metals traders have said concerns about Russian supply problems, sparked by a delay in Japan-Russia talks on export contracts, have been the main factor behind the recent rally in platinum group metal prices.
"It is interesting to note that if Russian platinum sales from stock were to be eliminated, then the platinum market could be between 5-10 percent short in terms of new supply.
"There would be several hundred thousand ounces short in a five million ounce market," said the Johannesburg analyst.
Irish Menell analyst George Topping said he believed Russia was holding out selling its metal to force higher prices.
"The Russians are not prepared to supply the quantities they were supplying at prices below $370," Topping added.
Analysts said Russian sales from stockpiles were estimated to be around 300,000 ounces a year.
Topping said "it all depends on the Russians".
"If the Russians do not have sufficient metal to meet the demand then there will be a shortage.

"If they haven't got that stock and are forced to cut back on their sales then that's a very different matter. Then I think you will see platinum rise much further than it has," he added. --Johannesburg newsroom, +27-11 482 1003
